## Which chart would you show the director? {#d3s2-p01 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

<div id="d8-labels">
<div data-variant>
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<div class="review-grid chart-pair"><div><h3>Chart A: draft</h3>',d8_bar(0,FALSE),'</div><div><h3>Chart B: draft</h3>',d8_bar(700,FALSE),'</div></div>'))
```
</div>
<div data-variant hidden>
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d8_pair())
```
</div>
</div>

<button data-swap="d8-labels" aria-controls="d8-labels" aria-pressed="false" data-closed="Reveal the labels and scales" data-opened="Hide the labels and scales">Reveal the labels and scales</button>

::: {.ask}
What is missing before you can choose a chart with confidence? After the reveal: what changes between Chart A and Chart B, and what stays the same?
:::

In a **bar chart**, the height of a bar shows an amount, so a baseline at zero usually keeps the comparison fair. **Worksheet page 3, Q1:** mark Figure C on page 1.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Predict before the reveal, then reveal the labels and scales on the same screen and compare. Both charts show the same data: the city participant businesses' mean annual waste management cost before and 12 months after GreenWaste (1,432 and 763 AED), not two groups. The incomplete drafts hide the values, units, group of businesses, time and scale. Chart B starts at 700 AED, so the bar-height ratio exaggerates the relative drop; the AED difference stays 669. Do not prohibit nonzero axes in every chart type. Judge the display against the claim and audience, not its drama. Participants mark Figure C on worksheet page 1 for Q1 (units, where each axis starts, group of businesses, time, comparison); the table of values behind the bars (Table C) is on that page. Source: H8-A Figure C, page 1. Start webR warming; no room poll required.
:::

## Describing a fall does not prove GreenWaste caused it. {#d3s2-p04 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

**Supported:** "The mean annual waste management cost of city participant businesses was about 669 AED lower 12 months after GreenWaste."

**Not shown by these bars:** "GreenWaste caused this fall" or "every participant's cost fell".

::: {.ask}
Q2 on page 3: write one statement that the bars support and one specific limit.
:::

The chart does not show a comparison that could support a causal reading, individual changes, or the uncertainty of an estimated effect.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Separate a mean change from a change for everyone, and description from causality. A causal claim needs a credible comparison; the individual claim needs paired changes. Baseline distributions alone cannot supply either. Reject generic "charts prove nothing": the means support specific descriptive facts. Do not attach another method's effect to these bars.
:::

## How much does the mean hide? {#d3s2-p05 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

```{webr}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Histogram of annual cost before GreenWaste, city participant businesses
hist(tp$cost_before, breaks = seq(0, 4500, 300), col = "#7da1c4",
     main = "", xlab = "Annual cost before GreenWaste (AED)",
     ylab = "Number of businesses")
abline(v = mean(tp$cost_before), col = "#B8272C", lwd = 3)
abline(v = median(tp$cost_before), col = "#063360", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Mean", "Median"), col = c("#B8272C", "#063360"),
       lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

::: {.ask}
Q3 on page 3: what does the histogram add to the single mean?
:::

Data: [evaluation_data_GreenWaste_simple.csv](https://3ie.academy/evaluation_data_GreenWaste_simple.csv) (fictional training records). Download it to explore.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. The trainer presses Run once; participants do not code. The chart includes all 4,794 city participant businesses' costs before GreenWaste in 300 AED bins from 0 to 4,500; none are excluded. Mean 1,432, median 1,376. Frequencies describe businesses, not effects. Reference: Figure D, page 2. If the browser is delayed, use Figure D on worksheet page 2. The data file is the same CSV that the code reads, so anyone can download it and run the code themselves.
:::

## Write a caption that fits what the chart shows. {#d3s2-p11 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

The draft caption beside the **bar charts** is: "GreenWaste substantially reduced every participant's costs."

In pairs, repair it in **Q5 on worksheet page 4**, for a director who is not a technical expert.

Your caption names the **group of businesses, the outcome, the units, the period, the comparison, the source and one limit on causal claims**.

::: {.ask}
Which baseline suits your corrected sentence, and why?
:::

::: {.notes}
9 minutes. Three minutes draft individually, four repair in pairs, two collect. Use Figure C/H8-A §1, not trial results. A valid caption names 4,794 participants, annual AED means 1,432 to 763, before/12 months after, with a causal limit. A zero bar baseline conveys relative magnitudes; justified alternative formats are acceptable. Collect annotation and caption, not a software drawing.
:::

## Variation and uncertainty are different kinds of spread. {#d3s2-p12 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

<div id="d8-pilot">
<div data-variant>
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d8_pilot(FALSE))
```
</div>
<div data-variant hidden>
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d8_pilot())
```
</div>
</div>

<button data-swap="d8-pilot" aria-controls="d8-pilot" aria-pressed="false" data-closed="Reveal the 95% interval" data-opened="Hide the 95% interval">Reveal the 95% interval</button>

::: {.ask}
Q6 on page 4: does this interval show that our rule of at least a 1,000 AED reduction is met? (Figure P, page 7)
:::

The interval shows **uncertainty about an estimated mean effect**, not the range of individual savings.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Separate pilot: 400 businesses, 200 in the treatment group and 200 in the control group, annual waste management cost in AED at 12 months. The estimate is 1,014 and the interval 862 to 1,167 includes values below 1,000. H8-A §4, Figure P, page 7. The interval is not an individual range or an allowance for all bias; the earlier histogram has a different meaning. Predict before revealing the interval. No new inference lecture.
:::

## A scatter plot shows every business, not only the mean. {#d3s2-p12b .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d8_scatter())
```

::: {.ask}
What does each point show? What does the gap between the two fitted lines show? Does the gap show that GreenWaste caused the fall?
:::

Each point is one business in a random sample of 400 city businesses. A point below the dashed line had a lower cost 12 months later. The lines summarise the points. They do not show cause.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Random sample of 400 of the 10,000 city businesses, so that the points stay readable. Horizontal axis: annual cost before GreenWaste. Vertical axis: annual cost 12 months later. Both axes use the same scale, so the dashed line is the "no change" line at 45 degrees. Fitted lines come from all participant businesses and all comparison businesses separately. Some costs after GreenWaste are below zero in the data file. We read the graph as it is and do not interpret those points here. The gap between the lines is a description of two groups, not proof of cause: that depends on the comparison, as in the earlier sessions.
:::

## A forest plot puts estimates and intervals on one axis. {#d3s2-p12c .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

```{webr}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Estimate and 95% interval from each method (AED), copied from the earlier analyses
res <- data.frame(
  method = c("Pilot lottery", "City: extra change (DiD)",
             "Jump near score 58", "City matched comparison"),
  estimate = c(1014, 812, 721, 1029),
  lower = c(862, 792, 498, 859), upper = c(1167, 833, 943, 1200))
y <- nrow(res):1
par(mar = c(4, 12, 1, 1))
plot(res$estimate, y, xlim = c(0, 1500), pch = 19, cex = 1.6, yaxt = "n",
     ylab = "", xlab = "Estimated reduction in annual cost per business (AED)")
segments(res$lower, y, res$upper, y, lwd = 4, col = "#215a9e")
abline(v = 1000, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#B8272C")  # our rule
axis(2, at = y, labels = res$method, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
```

::: {.ask}
Which intervals include 1,000 AED? Which method gives the strongest evidence for our rule, and why should we not simply average the four?
:::

Each line is a 95% interval. The dot is the estimate. The dashed line is our rule of at least 1,000 AED. The methods use different businesses and different comparisons.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. The trainer presses Run once; participants do not code. Four methods from the course: pilot lottery (400 pilot businesses), city difference between the two changes (DiD, 10,000 city businesses), jump near score 58 (businesses close to the cutoff) and city matched comparison (participants and similar businesses). The estimates and intervals are typed into a small table in the code, copied from the earlier sessions, because the methods themselves are not rerun in the browser; that is how a forest plot is usually drawn from a results table. The same plot appears in Day 2 Session 3. The dashed line is our rule of at least a 1,000 AED reduction in annual waste management cost per business per year. The city methods reuse the same records, so they are not independent confirmations. The DiD interval is narrow because it uses all 10,000 businesses, not because it is more credible. If the browser is delayed, use the Day 2 Session 3 slide.
:::

## AI Snapshot: which chart is fairer? {#d3s2-p13 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

**Naive prompt** (a prompt with no context, as a busy person might type it): **"Which of these two charts better represents the difference, and why?"** This response was written for the exercise. It is not a real AI answer.

<div class="ai-reading">
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<p>',gsub('\n\n','</p><p>',d8_ai,fixed=TRUE),'</p>'))
```
</div>

::: {.ask}
Page 5: check each sentence against Figure C and the draft claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
8 minutes. Stage 1 of the 15-minute Snapshot. Adapt the older chart-fairness response: accurate means plus unsupported truncation advice, causal effect and every-participant claims. Nonzero axes can be legitimate; assess context, not a blanket rule. Correct arithmetic does not justify the format or claim. Three minutes mark up, three compare, two debrief. The response was written for the exercise; it is not a real AI answer. Source pages 1-2 support the cost task.
:::

## Ask Copilot about the claim and its audience {#d3s2-p14 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

<div class="better-prompt">
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<strong>Improved prompt</strong><p>',d8_prompt,'</p>'))
```
</div>

::: {.ask}
Use the full prompt on page 5. Check one correction and one missing-evidence question.
:::

If you are not using Copilot, read the **prepared response on page 6** after Stage 1.

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. Stage 2 in Copilot, no account setup. Two minutes enter/run, three verify against §1, two share. The text source describes both baselines if images cannot be supplied. Use fictional course evidence only, not sensitive documents. The response should ask questions before recommending. No second-chat task. Different faithful caption wording is acceptable.
:::

## Defend your chart choice and state its limit. {#d3s2-p15 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

The director asks whether to approve the expansion. Use your repaired **caption for the bar chart** from Q5.

Explain:

- What the figure supports.
- Why its baseline fits that sentence.
- What further evidence the decision still needs.

::: {.ask}
Can a clearer chart supply the comparison that is missing?
:::

::: {.notes}
4 minutes. Each partner explains for one minute, then compare. Accept different faithful captions. Visual repair cannot create the missing comparison or effect uncertainty. Request causal and economic evidence suited to the expansion decision; do not substitute a pilot point estimate for the city's descriptive result.
:::

## What should you check before trusting a chart? {#d3s2-p16 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s2-review}

Close the source. In **Q7 on worksheet page 4**, write:

1. One check you would make first, and why.
2. One statement that the chart supports, and one limit.

::: {.ask}
Which error is your check designed to prevent?
:::

**Axes and labels. The group of businesses and the comparison. Variation between businesses versus uncertainty. The claim versus the evidence.**

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Two minutes independent writing, two pair challenge, one feedback. The annotated Figure C and Q5 caption are the main learning evidence; the memory check targets follow-up. Require a specific check, not general distrust of charts. Total 90 minutes, proposed 10:45-12:15 slot; the longer break follows.
:::
